{"candidate_slot":1,"current_prompt":"You will receive JSON with two parts: 'system_profile' (installed software inventory with names and versions) and 'advisories' (supplied CVE entries, each with an ID, description, and affected version information). Determine which supplied advisories actually affect the installed system. Only IDs from the supplied advisories list may appear in your answer.

For EVERY advisory, apply this procedure strictly and completely. Do not skip any advisory, and do not stop early.

STEP 1 — PRODUCT MATCH (normalize aggressively before concluding a product is absent).
Identify the affected product from the advisory's ID, description, and affected information. Product names appear in many styles: title-case marketing names ('ExampleProduct'), package-manager identifiers ('example-product', 'libexampleproduct'), underscore forms ('example_product'), and vendor-prefixed or vendor-stripped names ('Acme Example Product' vs 'example-product'). To match:
- Lowercase both names.
- Replace hyphens, underscores, and spaces with a single canonical separator (or remove separators entirely).
- Strip vendor/company prefixes and common package suffixes ('lib', 'software', 'core', 'package', 'runtime') before comparing.
- Compare on the core product name.
Package-manager-style identifiers (hyphenated, underscored, or lib-prefixed) are extremely common in system profiles — ALWAYS normalize them before deciding a product is absent. If the normalized product is not installed anywhere in system_profile, the advisory is NOT applicable — exclude it regardless of how severe or general the description sounds. The description is often misleading; the affected product/version information is authoritative.

STEP 2 — VERSION MATCH (this is where most errors happen; be meticulous).
If the product IS installed, compare the installed version against the advisory's affected range.
(a) PADDING: Pad the shorter version with zeros so both versions have equal segment counts before comparing numerically segment by segment (1.2 == 1.2.0.0; 3 == 3.0.0.0; 1.2.3 == 1.2.3.0; 2 == 2.0 == 2.0.0.0). A version with fewer segments than the bound is NOT automatically outside the range — pad first. Likewise, if the installed version has MORE segments than the bound (e.g., installed 1.2.3.4 against bound 1.2), pad the BOUND and compare. Never reject a candidate simply because segment counts differ.
(b) LOWER BOUNDS: If the advisory specifies a lower bound (greater_than / greater_than_or_equal, or prose like 'versions from X', 'X and later', 'affects versions X through Y'), the installed version must be at or above it (inclusive) or strictly above it (exclusive), respectively. A version BELOW a lower bound means NOT affected — check this direction explicitly. If there is NO lower bound, do not invent one: all versions up to the upper bound qualify.
(c) UPPER BOUNDS: 'versions prior to 2.0', 'before 2.0 (excluding 2.0)', 'up to and excluding 1.5.2', and less_than bounds are EXCLUSIVE — a version exactly equal to the endpoint is NOT affected. 'through 2.3', '2.3 and earlier', 'up to and including 2.3', and less_than_or_equal bounds are INCLUSIVE — a version exactly equal to the endpoint IS affected. Never exclude a version exactly on an inclusive endpoint; never include a version exactly on an exclusive endpoint.
(d) INTERVALS: For interval constraints (e.g., >= 1.0 and < 2.4.1), BOTH constraints must hold simultaneously. An installed version inside the interval is affected even if it is not mentioned in the prose.
(e) ALL INSTANCES: Check every installed instance of the product; if ANY installed instance falls inside the affected range, the advisory applies.
(f) SEMANTICS OVER PROSE: Convert prose ('prior to X', 'before X excluding X', 'through X', 'X and earlier', 'from X to Y') and structured fields (affected, less_than, less_than_or_equal, greater_than, greater_than_or_equal, inclusive/exclusive flags) into explicit inclusive/exclusive bounds before comparing. Treat both forms as equivalent evidence.

STEP 3 — DECISION RULE.
An advisory is applicable ONLY IF (a) its affected product is installed after normalization, AND (b) the installed version satisfies ALL affected-version constraints, including lower bounds. An advisory is NOT applicable if the product is absent OR any version constraint fails (too old for a lower bound, too new for an upper bound, exactly on an exclusive endpoint).

Common mistakes to avoid:
- Including an advisory because the product name looks installed without fully checking version constraints in BOTH directions.
- Excluding an advisory because the product name merely looks different due to alias style, vendor prefix, underscores, or hyphens.
- Misreading exclusive bounds as inclusive or inclusive bounds as exclusive.
- Failing to pad version segments before comparison, or assuming a 1- or 2-segment version cannot match a 3- or 4-segment bound (2 can equal 2.0.0.0).
- Assuming a 3-, 4-, or 5-segment installed version cannot be compared against a shorter bound — pad the bound.
- Excluding a version exactly on an inclusive endpoint, or including one exactly on an exclusive endpoint.
- Ignoring lower bounds: a version below a greater_than/greater_than_or_equal bound is NOT affected; a version at or above an inclusive lower bound and at or below the upper bound IS affected.
- Skipping advisories whose product is installed with a version clearly inside the stated range.

STEP 4 — OUTPUT.
Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing the unique identifiers (exactly as supplied, no alterations) of all applicable advisories, in any order. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output nothing else — no explanations, no markdown, no code fences, no extra keys, no trailing text. The response must be valid JSON parseable in its entirety. Every ID must come from the supplied advisories
